item.title: N.Y.C. Leaders Want Integrated Schools. Advocates Want a Plan.
item.description:
A few days before the start of school in September, Kamar Samuels stood before a room of lawyers in Manhattan and outlined his vision for New York City’s public schools. He wanted safe schools, academic rigor and a third goal that he said set him apart from his predecessor.

“I’m the first chancellor to come in and speak directly to school integration,” said Mr. Samuels, who offered few details at a New York Law School event before excusing himself for an engagement in Brooklyn with the mayor.

More than 10 months into his job overseeing the nation’s largest public school system, Mr. Samuels has barnstormed across the city, repeating his pledge to take on desegregation in school meetings, television interviews and legislative hearings. The goal is shared by the mayor, Zohran Mamdani, who called segregated schools a crisis during his campaign and selected a chancellor who in previous city positions had merged and closed schools in an effort to foster integration.

“We are speaking about the most segregated school system in the United States of America,” Mr. Mamdani said this week on WNYC’s “The Brian Lehrer Show,” referring to the findings of a landmark 2014 report that helped spur an integration movement in the city that fizzled in the pandemic.

While Mr. Mamdani and Mr. Samuels have spoken about desegregation with urgency, prominent integration proponents in the city say that their early optimism has turned into growing alarm. Nearly a year in, the administration’s rhetoric has not yielded a citywide integration plan or specifics on how it intends to pursue desegregation.

Nyah Berg, the executive director of New York Appleseed, a group that supports integrated schools, said that the administration’s approach reminded her of past efforts that had stalled when city leaders did not move from talking about integration to doing something.

“It’s not that I’m at the point of disappointment,” said Ms. Berg, who served on the mayor’s youth and education transition committee. “We are gravely concerned that this is not moving forward.”

In interviews with leading integration proponents and people close to the school system, all expressed broader concerns that while the Mamdani administration has laid out detailed plans on major issues like housing and universal child care, it has not released a comparable vision for education.

As is the case in only a handful of large American cities, New York’s mayor controls the public schools, which have many challenges, including shrinking enrollment and declining reading scores. Schools also play an enormous role in whether families stay in the city or move, and the school system’s roughly $40 billion budget is the largest of any city agency.

During the campaign, Mr. Mamdani did not release a comprehensive education agenda. As mayor, he still has not articulated one.

“The Bible says, ‘Without a vision, the people will perish,’” said NeQuan McLean, a parent leader in Bedford-Stuyvesant in Brooklyn. “So where’s the vision?”

The topic of segregated schools dominated conversation in education circles and far beyond last month after The New York Times Magazine reporter Nikole Hannah-Jones wrote about wrestling with her choice to send her daughter to a high-poverty elementary school in Brooklyn that was almost entirely Black and Latino. On Friday, New York Appleseed announced that it would hold a town-hall-style event about school integration with Ms. Hannah-Jones and Mr. Samuels later in October.

Still, while Mr. Mamdani and Mr. Samuels have brought more attention to segregation in the city’s schools than the previous mayor, they have only offered vague commitments to addressing it.

In June, Mr. Samuels created several neighborhood working groups responsible for issuing recommendations on topics that included smaller class sizes, under-enrolled schools and integration. New groups will be rolled out across the city during the next two years. In a citywide racial equity report released last month, Mr. Mamdani called for more integrated schools by 2034 without specific goals or next steps.

The city’s Department of Education has provided few details about the groups and has not released a list of members. (Mr. McLean said that he was serving on one and that his group would not address integration.) Integration advocates said that department officials had briefed them on the groups but that they were still unsure of their goals or how Mr. Samuels defines what he calls “true integration.”

“The working groups are one piece of the puzzle, but if that’s the only piece that they’re pursuing, that’s a problematic strategy,” said Matt Gonzales, a former member of a citywide school diversity advisory panel under former Mayor Bill de Blasio who also served on Mr. Mamdani’s transition committee.

Mr. Gonzales and other advocates called on Mr. Samuels to use the advisory panel’s recommendations as a blueprint for integration.

New York is among the most diverse cities in the country. But few of its more than 1,800 public schools reflect that diversity. Black and Hispanic students make up about 66 percent of the school system. About 14 percent are white, while 17 percent are Asian students. More than three-quarters of children come from low-income families.

Fewer than 2 percent of schools resemble the racial composition of the city, according to a new analysis from the Research Alliance for New York City Schools at New York University. At nearly half the schools, Black and Hispanic students make up more than 90 percent of the students.

The disparities are stark in its most coveted schools. Just 16 percent of the students at the five citywide gifted schools are Black and Hispanic, down a few points from before the pandemic. Those populations make up 13 percent of the city’s elite specialized high schools.

The school system has shifted in recent decades toward school choice for families, allowing students to attend schools outside their neighborhoods, and more gifted and screened schools, all of which have been blamed for worsening segregation. The number of middle schools with selective admissions was reduced several years ago. Some parts of the city have greatly reduced their screened schools, including a progressive part of Brooklyn that eliminated them for middle school.

Decades of research show that integration can lift educational and social outcomes for all children. Diverse schools are more likely to receive additional funding and resources. Still, racial segregation can persist inside diverse schools, studies show, with Black and Hispanic students having less access to advanced courses.

“What the research shows pretty compellingly is it only works when it’s associated with actually reallocating resources within the schools,” said Alexandra Freidus, an associate professor at the University of Connecticut who published a book last year on diversity efforts in New York City schools.

Mr. Mamdani has said he would phase out the gifted and talented program but no changes have been made. He recently said that the admissions test for specialized high schools should not change. (Mr. Mamdani graduated from one, the Bronx High School of Science.)

“We are exploring every single tool that we have at our disposal to ensure that this is going to be a very different school system moving forward,” he said on “The Brian Lehrer Show.”

In a way, integration advocates want to recapture the traction they had leading up to the pandemic, when another chancellor also made desegregation a signature issue. Back then, pressure on elected officials had mounted, led by activist groups and students, who had staged rallies, walkouts and lock-ins. Students planned to elevate the issue with a citywide walkout in April 2020. But when April arrived, school had moved to remote learning.

Since then, some groups have disbanded, those students have since graduated from college and the momentum has faded. Lawsuits challenging segregation have been tossed. Past promises and recommendations went unrealized.

Any effort by the Mamdani administration to integrate schools would undoubtedly touch on thorny issues and popular programs in the school system. It would also face fierce resistance from some parents. And there are entrenched barriers: Only about a third of the school system’s districts reflect the demographics of the city.

Kathryn Hill, the research director at the Research Alliance for New York City Schools, said that a citywide integration effort could require sweeping but potentially unpopular changes.

“If the system really wanted to push integration, they probably would have to redraw community school district boundary lines or school catchment areas,” Dr. Hill said.

Bianca Pallaro contributed reporting.

item.title: 20 Chestnut Trees: A Cause for Celebration at the Bronx Zoo
item.description:
Good morning. It’s Monday. We’ll find out why 20 trees that will be planted today matter to the Bronx Zoo. We’ll also get details about the weekend at Cornell University.

The Bronx Zoo is about to address a problem it discovered so long ago that Abdul, its Aldabra tortoise, hadn’t been born yet. At around 100, he is one of the zoo’s oldest residents.

Even when Abdul was young, the American chestnut trees on the zoo’s 265-acre grounds were in trouble, the result of a blight that ultimately destroyed more than four billion trees across the country. The culprit was identified in 1904 — 20 or so years before Abdul was born — by the zoo’s chief forester at the time.

Craig Piper, the current director of the zoo, told me that he did not know when the last American chestnut at the zoo died. History suggests it was probably when Abdul was a teenager.

Today, in a moment that is sure to be freighted with meaning, the zoo will plant 20 new chestnut trees, the first it has brought in since the blight all but wiped out the species. “This is so much more than planting trees to us,” Piper told me last week, when we talked about why planting a mere 20 trees mattered. “Our overall mission is about conserving wildlife,” he said, “but to do that, we have to conserve the place.”

These days, it’s hard to imagine why Henry David Thoreau referred to “boundless chestnut woods” in “Walden” or that the chestnuts roasting on an open fire in “The Christmas Song” were probably American chestnuts. But American chestnuts were, in fact, once a dominant species — “a defining part of our forests,” according to Lynn Bodnar Kelly, the executive director of the New York Restoration Project, a nonprofit that has worked for years to bring back American chestnuts.

Piper — who is also the interim executive vice president of the Wildlife Conservation Society, which runs the Bronx Zoo — said that American chestnuts had been “a primary food source for bears as they were bulking up for the wintertime, for deer, squirrels, chipmunks. The nuts were important forage for farm animals.” The wood was prized for cabinets and furniture as well as for boats, fences and telephone poles.

Then the fungus arrived, probably with Asian chestnut trees that were imported, and spread with surprising speed. Hermann Merkel, the zoo’s chief forester in the early 1900s, wrote in 1905 that the disease had appeared “in a few scattered cases which occurred during the summer of 1904. Since that time, however, it has spread to such an extent that today it is no exaggeration to say that 98 percent of all the chestnut trees in the parks of this borough are infected.”

The new chestnuts are hybrids that have been bred to resist the tree-killing fungus. The American Chestnut Foundation developed them using traditional breeding methods to generate trees with the blight resistance of Chinese chestnuts and the strength of the original American species.

“We think it’s a good time to be planting trees in New York,” said Jason Smith, the director of northern Manhattan parks for the New York Restoration Project. The group is donating the hybrids to the zoo in partnership with the American Chestnut Foundation.

His group, working with the city’s Department of Parks and Recreation, planted a grove in Highbridge Park in Upper Manhattan nearly 10 years ago. More recently, with the Brooklyn conservationist Bart Chezar and the American Chestnut Foundation, it has run the “1,000 Chestnut Challenge,” which makes chestnuts available to New Yorkers willing to plant them.

For the zoo, the planting amounts to coming full circle. “The Bronx Zoo was a part of this whole tragic story,” Smith said. “I think they’re eager for a happy ending.”

Weather

Temperatures will rise near 69 today, as partly sunny skies make way for the sun. Expect clear skies tonight and a low near 50.

ALTERNATE-SIDE PARKING

In effect until Oct. 12 (Indigenous Peoples’ Day).

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“All holy places. All places where I find quiet.” — Christopher Myers, on the Nuyorican Poets Cafe, the Studio Museum in Harlem and the Cathedral of St. John the Divine. He created a picture book that follows five young people who explore the city by bike in the dark.

An antidote to glassy, gray buildings: Antonio Echeverri bought an East Village building in 1992 and in the early 2000s painted it bright colors. He has just given it a refresh with colors that look pink in sunlight and lavender under clouds as a tribute to the human palette of New York. “All of us,” he says.

Unofficial Statue of Liberty boat tours: Lawmakers want to curb what they call deceptive tactics used to dupe unsuspecting visitors seeking an up-close experience at the Statue of Liberty. Sellers say they are serving a market, but often ticket buyers cannot step onto Liberty Island.

Porch concerts in Brooklyn: At the height of the Covid-19 pandemic, Aaron Lisman started what became Operation Gig, a porch concert series to build community and help musicians. Operation Gig now offers him a front-row seat for exceptional concerts and lets him hang out with the talent.

Exploring a subway tragedy: Anand Giridharadas’s new book, “Man in the Mirror,” explores the fatal meeting between Jordan Neely, a homeless and mentally ill Michael Jackson impersonator, and Daniel Penny, an ex-Marine.

At Cornell University, shaken by last week’s revelations about how the campus police and the local district attorney had handled a sophomore’s claim that she was raped at a fraternity party in 2024, the weekend was subdued. My colleague Maia Coleman writes that there was a sense of heaviness, and many students stayed away from large parties.

“It felt like you had to take a break from it — the story has kind of been all-consuming,” said Hal Stokes, a senior. He and a friend went to a local hangout that serves food and coffee and operates a small bar in search of a low-key night.

By the end of last week, there was a high-profile criminal investigation, with Letitia James, the state attorney general, overseeing it. Gov. Kathy Hochul assigned James to the case after denouncing the local district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, who decided not to bring charges in 2024. Documents obtained by The New York Times showed last week that a summary from the campus police forwarded to Van Houten did not contain the statement by the Cornell sophomore at the center of the case, who said she had been raped.

As the week ended, many at Cornell voiced sympathy for her, or outrage. Others defended the men she accused in a civil lawsuit. They have denied the allegations.

Some students wonder what’s next for Cornell — and whether a university that finds itself uncomfortably in the national spotlight will ever be the same. As Lewis Holland, a senior, put it, his voice shaking, “Cornell is now known for this.”

METROPOLITAN diary

Dear Diary:

About 20 years ago, I flew into New York from Houston for a conference followed by several fun days with a friend who worked in the city and lived in Mamaroneck.

One night, we went to a flamenco show on St. Marks Place. The performances were amazing, and long. We had to hustle back to Grand Central to avoid missing the last train.

Passing under a streetlight, I noticed a vintage 1970s bicycle chained to the fence outside a brownstone. The back of the big, padded seat looked familiar, as did the silhouette of the handlebars and, upon a close look, the distinctive double-down tubes.

I called ahead to my friend to wait, and examined the blue-green paint, built-in headlamp and chrome fenders over the big wheels. I gripped the handlebars, straddled the heavy bike and placed my seat and feet into position. Long-dormant muscle memory flooded back.

Finally, I peered at the seat post and confirmed my suspicion: a remnant of a City of Houston bicycle registration decal. It was the Skyrider Deluxe my parents had given me for Hanukkah in 1970.

It had moved from California to Houston and had then most likely been bought by a collector when my mother sold the house. All those years later, my old queen of a bicycle made sure I saw it in Manhattan.

I left a scrap of paper with my scribbled name, a quick story and a plea for the owner to contact me before ever selling.

We did catch the train, and I called my father in Houston.

“I’ll be damned,” is all he said. “I’ll be damned.”

— Rachel Dvoretzky

Illustrated by Agnes Lee. Tell us your New York story here and read more Metropolitan Diary here.

Glad we could get together here. See you tomorrow. — J.B.

Davaughnia Wilson and Ed Shanahan contributed to New York Today. You can reach the team at nytoday@nytimes.com.

item.title: A Building Is Vandalized at Cornell as Week of Protest Begins
item.description:
Vandals shattered a glass door and sprayed graffiti on Cornell University’s main administration building early on Monday, in a turbulent start to a week of planned protest of the way the university handled allegations of sexual assault at a fraternity.

The door to the five-story building, Day Hall, was smashed, with two large holes visible and shards of glass covering the ground. On one side of the door graffiti in red paint read: “At Cornell rapists are protected protesters are expelled.” On the other side, also in graffiti, were the words: “Smash the patriarchy.”

The Cornell administration said the vandalism was under investigation.

“We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community,” Kyle Kimball, vice president for university relations, said. “Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer. We are investigating the vandalism at Day Hall and will address it in accordance with university policy and applicable law.”

The middle-of-the-night vandalism was the starkest demonstration of anger on campus since a woman’s lawsuit detailing allegations of sexual assault at a fraternity party ignited outrage around the country.

It comes ahead of a “Justice for Survivors” protest planned for Monday by 20 student organizations calling for sexual assault prevention. On Wednesday, some student groups are planning to skip class and hold a seven-hour sit-in in solidarity with the woman, known as Jane Doe, who has said she was plied with drugs and raped by several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Oct. 19, 2024. Last month, the woman sued seven men, the university, Chi Phi and her sorority.

The protests follow an emotional week on campus, as students expressed frustration with the way the administration and law enforcement handled the sexual assault allegations. Many students have questioned why some of the men accused of sexual assault had been permitted to remain on campus.

While the identity of the vandals was not known, a group whose members referred to themselves as “autonomous activists” released a statement on Monday taking credit for the action and accusing Cornell of using “its power and resources to protect rather than condemn sexual violence.”

The 2024 incident at the fraternity, the activists wrote, was part of a “rampant pattern of sexual assault perpetrated by members of Greek life at Cornell University and hundreds of other academic institutions throughout the country.”

The Cornell Police Department did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Last week, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed a special prosecutor, Attorney General Letitia James, to investigate Jane Doe’s allegations.

All the accused students have denied wrongdoing, and none have been charged with a crime.

The New York Times reported on Saturday that two of the seven men were expelled, two more were suspended and another was barred from campus. The remaining two students received lighter punishments. The university, the fraternity and prosecutors have said they responded appropriately given the information they had.

The administrative building that the vandals targeted has been at the center of campus activism for decades, serving as the site of a takeover by Latino Studies advocates in 1993.

It was not the first incident of vandalism at Cornell related to the events at the fraternity, Chi Phi. In November 2024, after reports of a rape accusation at the fraternity surfaced and the fraternity was suspended, a student activist group smashed the windows and spray painted the exterior of the building, The Cornell Daily Sun reported.

Since last week, when the Tompkins County district attorney announced he was reopening the investigation into Jane Doe’s allegations, Cornell has been forced to grapple with the cloud that the allegations have cast over the university.

The vandalism at the building was the latest example of visible anger over the school’s handling of various on-campus issues.

Since 2024, at least 15 students have been suspended for their activism around the Israel-Hamas war. In April, after a group of students surrounded his vehicle to protest the university’s suspension of the activists, the university president, Michael Kotlikoff, bumped a student with his car.

The language in the activists’ statement on Monday echoed that of the pro-Palestinian activists who have been a fixture of Cornell’s protest scene for the last two years. Among references to the Palestinian cause and “global violence against women” in countries like South Africa and India, it connected support for Jane Doe with a struggle for “all lives being squashed by the American empire.”

The activists, in their statement, denounced what they viewed as a double standard concerning the suspension of pro-Palestinian students and the punishment meted out to the men accused by Jane Doe. One of the pro-Palestinian activists was banned from campus after graduation, while two of the men accused by Jane Doe had to write essays and undergo sexual harassment training.

item.title: Punishments at Cornell
item.description:
Good morning. Protests are planned to start at Cornell University today and are expected to continue this week. An administration building was defaced and a glass door smashed early this morning.

The school’s president called the inquiry into Jane Doe’s rape allegations a “defining moment” for the school. And Jane Doe’s lawyer said in an interview with NBC News that she was “not doing well.”

We have more about how Cornell disciplined the men accused of sexual assault in Jane Doe’s lawsuit. None of the men face criminal charges. All of them denied any wrongdoing. Read their accounts of the night here.

In university disciplinary records obtained by The Times, we found:

The school expelled two of the men. A university panel found one responsible for sexual assault, according to the records. Another, the files show, sent a Snapchat message to fraternity members encouraging them to enter the bedroom where Jane Doe was undressed. She also accused him of sexual assault.

The university suspended two of the men and put them on probation. Jane Doe had accused one of them of inhaling ketamine off her body and forcing oral sex on her. He was suspended for two years. Jane Doe alleged that the other man had sex with her without her consent. He was suspended for three semesters. Both were required not to contact Jane Doe. They were also required to study sexual harassment and to write reflection papers, according to disciplinary records.

Jane Doe accused one man of forcibly kissing her. He had graduated by the time of the discipline panel’s ruling, but he faced a persona non grata order and was barred from campus for three years, according to the files.

Two others were accused of being part of the group of men who entered the room after reading a Snapchat message, the records show. The school ordered them not to contact Jane Doe; to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention; and to write reflection papers, the documents show.

Read the full story.

The campus was subdued, even as some students were still looking to cut loose.

“I think that it’s going to be a quieter year,” one senior, reflecting on the pause on Greek life this weekend, told my colleague Maia Coleman. “The vibe is different, at least for us. I would be very surprised if in a week, two weeks, three weeks, we were back to normal.”

What you need to know to be the smartest person in class today.

1. It’s the first day of a new Supreme Court term. The first case is a landmark dispute about whether local governments can sue oil companies over damages caused by climate change. Follow our live coverage.

2. Democrats are leading governor races in Republican territory, according to new polls. They are in reach of flipping four Republican-held governorships in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas.

3. The U.S. rushed to withdraw bombers from a British air base. The withdrawal was highly unusual, and it came after new threats about an Iran-backed plot against the installation.

4. The Nobel Prizes are being announced this week. Three scientists were awarded the prize in physiology or medicine today for their discoveries in neuroscience.

5. Karoline Leavitt has a new gig. The former White House press secretary is joining Fox News as a contributor.

What you’re wearing.

Who: Jayden Morfín, 20, mechanical engineering major at the University of Arkansas.

The details: I’m known for wearing pajama pants on the regular, and that day a group of resident assistants and I decided to dress formally for our staff meeting, just because (hence the sports jacket).

Submit your outfits to Fit Check.

The American University of Afghanistan has lost its State Department funding, putting the education of hundreds of Afghan women at risk.

The Times’s publisher, A.G. Sulzberger, spoke with student journalists at Michigan State University. Read his interview with The State News.

Five fraternities at Indiana University were placed on cease and desist in September after allegations of hazing. (Indiana Daily Student)

The campus Wi-Fi at the University of South Carolina is reportedly bad. (The Daily Gamecock)

The stories about to hit your group chat

Can you tell if this music is A.I. generated? My colleague spent days making a song to compare. (I preferred the song made by humans. How about you?) Read more about the experiment here.

Librarians are keeping communities together. We spoke to more than 50 of them about their jobs. I found their responses so moving.

What are the best TV shows? You let us know. More than 100,000 people told us their favorite shows of the century so far. See the full list. (And how well do you know them? Take our quiz.)

Do this to get ahead.

Make this sandwich. You need only three ingredients: a baguette, butter and ham.

Tell the truth. Giving someone feedback can be a challenge, but it’s doable. Here are some tips.

Take our news quiz. How much did you keep up with the headlines last week? Test your knowledge.

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U.S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

And forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T.A. See you tomorrow!

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that includes top headlines and analysis.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes.com

The editor of Extra Credit is Lauren Jackson. Brent Lewis was our photo editor.

item.title: How Cornell Punished Each of the 7 Men Accused of Sexual Assault
item.description:
The lightest punishment called for writing a paper and completing training. The most severe was expulsion from the school.

After a woman attending Cornell University accused seven fraternity members of sexually assaulting her in 2024, the university convened a closed proceeding to determine what had occurred and whether those men should face discipline.

Since then, the sanctions imposed on each of the men, and the reasoning behind those decisions, have remained secret. The school has said little.

But detailed summaries of the punishments obtained by The New York Times provide the first look at how Cornell administrators apportioned blame for the alcohol and drug-fueled gathering that the woman has said left her shattered and degraded.

Two of the fraternity members were expelled. Another, who had already graduated, was barred from campus. Two more were suspended. The remaining men were handed lighter punishments, the summaries show.

All of them have denied any wrongdoing, and the Tompkins County district attorney declined to prosecute in 2024. None of the men have been charged with a crime. Their fraternity, Chi Phi, has been banned from campus.

Still, since allegations from the woman who has become known as Jane Doe surfaced in a lawsuit on Sept. 16, they have touched off intense anger over sexual abuse on campus and why more is not done to punish those responsible. Others have criticized what they see as a rush to judge the seven men involved.

In her lawsuit, Jane Doe claimed that, from the start of her encounter involving the seven fraternity members, she was incapable of consent because she was severely intoxicated. The lawsuit inflamed particular ire by stating that the defendants were all “afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell,” an assertion Cornell has said did not accurately reflect what occurred.

Combined with more than 1,000 pages of interview transcripts, police reports and other records gathered by Cornell investigators and previously obtained by The Times, the discipline summaries show that the university based its decisions on a broad and complicated body of evidence.

In the end, the punishments handed out by the three-member panel, which met on Zoom over 12 days in May 2025, varied widely. The panel, which enforces federal civil rights at the university under Title IX provisions, did not conclude that Jane Doe was sexually assaulted by all the men she had accused, according to the discipline summaries.

The university investigative files outline in excruciating detail what the fraternity members were accused of doing on the night of Oct. 19, 2024.

It was Matthew Ingalls whom Jane Doe originally went to visit at the Chi Phi fraternity house at about 11 p.m. She walked there alone from a bar to see him, with her intoxication level from drinking through the evening at about a 5 out of 10, she told investigators.

After she arrived, Mr. Ingalls asked her if she wanted to have a threesome with Jonathan Newell, Jane Doe said. During that encounter, she said, the men gave her ketamine and alcohol. Eventually, other men engaged in sex acts with her without her consent and while she was incapacitated, she said.

At the end of the night at the fraternity house, when Jane Doe was near hallucinating, there was more sex, she told investigators.

Expulsions were handed to Mr. Ingalls and Mr. Newell — the man who sent a Snapchat message to other fraternity members encouraging them to enter the bedroom where Jane Doe was undressed, the discipline summaries show.

The discipline summaries show that the panel found Mr. Ingalls responsible for sexual assault, judging that he was willing to manipulate, exploit and endanger Jane Doe for his own self-interest and the entertainment of others.

A lawyer for Mr. Ingalls declined to comment.

Mr. Newell was also accused of sexual assault, the university files show. Jane Doe told police on Nov. 14, 2024, that he had struck her buttocks with enough force during intercourse to leave bruises, and that he had manipulated her to ingest ketamine.

It was not clear whether Mr. Newell had hired a lawyer, and he did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Suspensions and disciplinary probation were given to Winston Lee and Gillio Lopes. Jane Doe had accused Mr. Lee of inhaling ketamine off her body and forcing oral sex on her. She alleged that Mr. Lopes had sex with her without her consent.

Mr. Lee was suspended for two years, with several semesters of disciplinary probation upon his return; Mr. Lopes received a three-semester suspension and two years of probation, the discipline summaries show. Both men also were ordered not to contact Jane Doe, and were required to study sexual harassment and to write reflection papers.

Lawyers for Mr. Lee and Mr. Lopes did not respond to requests for comment.

A persona non grata order was issued to Diego Sarabia, who had graduated by the time of the discipline panel’s ruling. Mr. Sarabia, whom Jane Doe accused of forcibly kissing her, was barred from campus for three years.

The remaining two men, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar, were ordered not to contact Jane Doe, to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and to write “reflection papers.” They were accused of being part of a group of men who entered the room after reading Mr. Newell’s Snapchat message.

A recently unsealed lawsuit filed by Mr. Kretzschmar against Cornell shows that he was not found responsible for sexual assault. Instead, Cornell ruled that he had committed a lesser offense of attempted sexual exploitation.

Jeremy Saland, a lawyer for Mr. Kretzschmar, said in a statement on Friday that the discipline his client received showed that he was “never accused of, nor found responsible for, rape.”

“He was not even present during any sexual activity,” Mr. Saland said.

It was not clear whether Mr. Norris was represented by a lawyer, and phone calls and text messages to numbers listed for him and his family members went unanswered.

Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said in a statement on Friday that the punishments “did not reflect the severity of the charges.”

“With the exception of two of these men, all of them will be able to graduate with a Cornell diploma and live their lives reaping the benefits of this coveted degree,” Mr. Giuffra said. “In contrast, as of today, it is doubtful whether Ms. Doe will even graduate college or ever live a normal life due to what these men did to her.”

A spokeswoman for Cornell declined to comment, citing federal laws protecting student privacy.

Earlier this week, and in the wake of Jane Doe’s lawsuit, Gov. Kathy Hochul ordered an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the case. On Thursday, she appointed the New York State attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor with the power to bring criminal charges.
